svg.text: Largest prime factors of n and n + 1
Exact sieve of P(n) for every n up to 109 + 1, against the joint Dickman law ρ(1/a) ρ(1/b).
share of n in each 0.05 x 0.05 cell
product of the two marginal laws
C. Who has the larger P?
share of 2 ≤ n ≤ X with P(n) < P(n+1)
D. Independence ratio #{P(n) ≤ na and P(n+1) ≤ na} / (expected if independent)
observed joint count over product of the two observed marginal counts; the law says the ratio tends to 1
Total variation, panel A vs B: 0.055
Finite data illustrate, they do not prove: the approach to the limit is logarithmically slow. At 109 the smooth marginal is still below ρ(2),
primes put visible extra mass on the top row and right column (an atom of size about 1/log n that vanishes in the limit), and the a = 1/3 ratio is 0.77.
Counts are exact (integer tests P(n)2 ≤ n, P(n)3 ≤ n); cells use floating logs. Sieve: sieve012.c; picture: gen012.py.
